claims.text: Adding a minor amount of boron to phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys will improve glass-forming ability.
Adding boron will improve the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
Boron will promote a more interconnected short-range-ordered atomic network.
Conventional melt-quenching of the baseline phosphorus-containing alloy yields an amorphous structure.
The proposed boron concentration is approximately 1–3 atomic percent.
The beneficial effect requires uniform mixing.
Excessive boron can form separate boride phases.
Boron enhances icosahedral short-range order or crosslinked atomic clusters.
The enhanced clusters reduce free volume.
Reduced free volume and enhanced clustering slow atomic mobility.
Boron modifies the local bonding environment in the melt by promoting stronger local short-range order.
Stronger local short-range order kinetically hinders atomic rearrangements during cooling and subsequent thermal exposure.
The proposed modification increases the critical cooling rate for glass formation.
The proposed modification raises the onset temperature for crystallization.
The boron-doped alloy will have a higher critical casting thickness than the boron-free baseline.
The boron-doped alloy will require a lower critical cooling rate than the boron-free baseline.
The boron-doped alloy will have a higher DSC crystallization-onset temperature than the boron-free baseline.
The predicted improvements require rapid-quench conditions that produce a primarily amorphous structure.
Slow cooling, nonuniform mixing, or excessive boron may cause phase separation or boride precipitation and negate the beneficial effects.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says boron increases the critical cooling rate for glass formation, whereas the predicted outcome says it lowers the required critical cooling rate. Improved glass-forming ability ordinarily corresponds to a lower required critical cooling rate, so these directions conflict.
